title: Flu Season Starts Early in the U.S.
summary:
This year's flu season has started early, and it is spreading fast. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said on Friday that seven states were reporting high flu activity last week, up from two states the week before. Louisiana is seeing the worst of it so far.

Flu season is taking off, said Dr. Fred Lopez, an infectious diseases specialist in New Orleans, and it is only likely to increase in the next month or two. He urged everyone who has not been vaccinated to get vaccinated now.

The early activity is higher than usual for this time of year. The CDC estimates that at least 2.6 million people have already fallen ill with flu this season, with 36,000 hospitalisations and 2,100 deaths tied to the virus. In mid-October, the flu hospitalisation rate was the highest seen that early in autumn in more than 15 years, said Dr. Anna Durbin of Johns Hopkins University.

The surge began in the South and West. States with high flu activity so far include California, Louisiana, Oregon, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Washington. Louisiana is often among the first states to see flu surges, Lopez said, partly because of low vaccination rates and difficulty getting health care.

Doctors expect flu and other respiratory viruses to spread faster as people travel and gather for Thanksgiving later this month. Most illnesses so far are caused by a version of the H1N1 flu bug with changes that may help it slip past the body's defences, but early data suggests the current vaccine can recognise the circulating virus and work against it, said Andrew Pekosz, an immunology expert at Johns Hopkins. Lopez said people should still get a flu shot even if they already caught flu this autumn, because the vaccine protects against three kinds of flu virus.
why_it_matters: Flu is spreading earlier and faster than usual, so getting vaccinated now can protect many people before holiday travel brings more people together.

background_read: Flu is an illness caused by a virus that spreads from person to person, often through coughs and sneezes.
It can cause fever, cough, and body aches, and it can be serious for some people.
A flu vaccine teaches the body to recognise the flu virus and fight it off.
Flu spreads more easily when many people travel and gather indoors in colder months.
